newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian political parties agree crisis programme.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian political parties agree crisis programme.

text.p: More than 200 Bulgarian army officers angry at low wages gathered outside the presidency on Monday as political leaders drew up a crisis programme for a new caretaker cabinet.

Leaders of the political parties represented in parliament agreed to speed up privatisation, close loss-making state firms, crack down on corruption and the grey economy, and encourage investment, an official statement said.
Vesselin Metodiev of the opposition People's Union said all the political parties in parliament had agreed at a meeting with Stoyanov that they would not use the crisis for their political advantage.

Metodiev told reporters the parties had also agreed to support legislation to give the caretaker government a mandate to negotiate with international lenders, which the majority Socialists had previously opposed.
"For the first time there is a common outlook for the reforms in the country from all parliamentary groups," said Hristo Ivanov of the small Bulgarian Business Bloc.

The army officers, from the defence ministry, the military acdemy and other units around Sofia, complained that the outgoing cabinet had increased their salaries by only 60 percent last week while other state salaries were doubled.

National radio said officers at the military academy in Sofia had boycotted classes on Monday in protest. "This is in violation of the Defence and Armed Forces Law and could lead to riots in the army," the radio quoted them as saying.
According to the Defence Law, officers should be paid at least double the average state salary.

Official figures put inflation for the first 25 days of January at 43.8 percent, compared with 26.9 percent in the whole of December. The Confederation of Independent Trade Unions said food prices had risen by 242 percent since the beginning of the year.
Critics of the outgoing Socialist government blame much of the crisis on its corruption and reluctance to carry out reforms prescribed by international lenders.

The Socialists agreed last week after 30 days of nationwide protests to give up trying to form a cabinet. Stoyanov is expected to appoint a caretaker cabinet this week to govern until after elections in mid-April.
Bulgaria's biggest oil refinery has cut oil volumes to the critical minimum because it lacks cash for crude supplies. Most petrol stations are closed for lack of fuel.
Assen Dobryanov, deputy director of Sofia city transport, said fuel shortages might force them to reduce services in early morning and late evening but they would keep up rush hour services.
An opinion poll published on Monday showed the opposition coalition, which organised 30 days of mass protests, would win two thirds of parliamentary seats if elections were held now.

The poll by the NOEMA agency gave the Socialists 14.2 percent, and the main opposition Union of Democratic Forces 53.3 percent, plus 11.3 percent for its coalition allies, giving a total of 64.6 percent.
